source_text: ἑκάστου τρυβλίον ἓν ἀργυροῦν, καὶ φιάλη μία, καὶ ἀμφότερα, φησὶ, πλήρη σεμιδάλεως ἀναπεποιημένης ἐν ἐλαίῳ, θυΐσκη μία θυμιάματος ἔμπλεως, κριὸς εἷς, ἀμνὸς εἷς ἐνιαύσιος εἰς ὁλοκαύτωμα, χίμαρος ἐξ αἰγῶν περὶ ἁμαρτίας· καὶ ταυτὶ μὲν τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα. Προσεκόμιζον δὲ καὶ εἰς θυσίαν σωτηρίου, φησὶ, δαμάλεις δύο, κριοὺς πέντε, τράγους πέντε, ἀμνάδας ἐνιαυσίους πέντε. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Φράζε δὴ οὖν καὶ πρό γε τῶν ἄλλων, τί τὸ μεταξὺ, καὶ ποίαν ἄν τις εἴποι τὴν διαφορὰν τῆς τοῦ σωτηρίου θυσίας, καὶ ὁλοκαυτώματος. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἄκουε δή. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὁλοκαυτώματα τῶν ζώων ὅλα δι' ὅλων, ἱερῷ καὶ ἀσβέστῳ κατεφλέγετο πυρὶ, οὐδενὸς τὸ σύμπαν ἐξῃρημένου, ἀλλ' οἱονεί πως παντὸς μορίου καὶ μέλους εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας ἀναβαίνοντος τῷ. θεῷ, τὰ δέ γε ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ σωτηρίου θυσίας σφαζόμενα, μερικὴν ἐδέχετο τὴν καθιέρωσιν, ὡς ἐν ὤμῳ δεξιῷ, κεφαλῇ τε καὶ ποσὶ, νεφροῖς καὶ ἥπατι, καὶ ἑτέροις τισὶ τοῖς εἰς τὸ εἴσω καὶ ἐνδοσθίοις. Πρέπει δὴ οὖν τὸ ὁλοκαυτοῦσθαι Χριστῷ· καὶ γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὅλος ἅγιος, εὐώδης ἅπας καὶ ἱερός. Ἡμῖν δὲ οἰκεῖον, τὸ οὐκ εἰσάπαν ἅγιον, καὶ οὐχ ὁλοκλήρως ἱερὸν, οἷς ἔνεστί τι καὶ μολυσμοῦ διὰ τὴν ἐν ἡμῖν ἁμαρτίαν. «Καθαρὸς γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἀπὸ ῥύπου,» καὶ «Παραπτώματα τίς συνήσει;» κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον. Διὰ τοῦτο τὴν ὑπὲρ τοῦ σωτηρίου θυσίαν, οὐχ ὁλόκαυτον ὁ νόμος, μερικῶς δὲ μᾶλλον καθιεροῦσθαι δεῖν εὖ μάλα προστέταχεν. Ἆρ' οὖν, ὦ Παλλάδιε, σαφής σοι καὶ ἀποχρῶν εἰς εὐμαθίαν ὁ λόγος; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Καὶ μάλα. {ΚΥΡ.} Φέρε δὴ οὖν, ἐπ' ἐκεῖνο ἴωμεν εἴς γε τὸ, ἑκάστῳ φημὶ τῶν προσενηνεγμένων, φάναι τι, καὶ μὴν καὶ συνιέναι τῶν ἀναγκαίων εἰς ὄνησιν. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἴθι δὴ οὖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἔστι τοίνυν τὰ παρ' ἑκάστου τῶν φυλάρχων, τρυβλίον ἀργυροῦν ἓν καὶ φιάλη μία, καὶ ἀμφότερα πλήρη σεμιδάλεως ἀναπεποιημένης ἐλαίῳ. Τὸ μὲν οὖν τρυβλίον ἐστὶ τοῖς ἐδωδίμοις ὑπηρετοῦν, καὶ εἰς ὀψοφαγίαν χρήσιμον, καθὸ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδίδαξεν ὁ Σωτὴρ φιλοπνευστοῦντι Ἰωάννῃ τῷ γνησίῳ μαθητῇ τίς ὁ παραδώσων αὐτὸν, «Ὁ ἐμβάψας, φησὶ, μετ' ἐμοῦ τὴν χεῖρα ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ.» Φιάλης δὲ τί ἂν λέγοιμι τὴν χρείαν, διακεκραγότος ὡδὶ τοῦ πράγματος; Καὶ σημεῖον ἄρτου σεμίδαλις, ὅτι καὶ ἐξ αὐτῆς ἄρτος, ἄρτος δὲ ζωῆς, ὁ Χριστός. Οὐκοῦν ὡς ἐν τῷ τρυβλίῳ καὶ ἐν τῇ φιάλῃ, καὶ ὡς ἐν ἄρτῳ τῷ ἐν ἀμφοῖν, πλήρη γὰρ ἦν σεμιδάλεως, ὡς ἐν βρώσει τε καὶ πόσει, ζωὴ καὶ ζωοποιὸς ὁ Χριστὸς σημαίνεται. «Ἀμὴν γὰρ, φησὶ, λέγω ὑμῖν, ἐὰν μὴ φάγητε τὴν σάρκα τοῦ Υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, καὶ πίητε αὐτοῦ τὸ αἷμα, οὐκ ἔχετε ζωὴν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.» Ἐλαίῳ δὲ τὴν σεμίδαλιν καταδεδεῦσθαί φησιν, αὐτό που τὸ ἐν Ψαλμοῖς ἀναμελῳδοῦντος οἱονεί που τοῦ τύπου· «Ἠγάπησας δικαιοσύνην, καὶ ἐμίσησας ἀδικίαν, διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεός σου ἔλαιον
pass_a_gloss: [Cont. of Cyril, after 'Then from'] each one silver dish (τρυβλίον), and one bowl/cup (φιάλη), and both, it says, full of fine flour (σεμίδαλις) kneaded-up (ἀναποιέω, perf. pass. ptc.) in oil; one incense-dish (θυΐσκη) full of incense (θυμίαμα); one ram (κριός), one yearling lamb (ἀμνὸς ἐνιαύσιος) for whole-burnt-offering (ὁλοκαύτωμα); a he-goat from the goats (χίμαρος ἐξ αἰγῶν) for sin (περὶ ἁμαρτίας); and these are the whole-burnt-offerings. And they brought for sacrifice of salvation (θυσία σωτηρίου), it says, two heifers (δάμαλις), five rams, five he-goats (τράγος), five yearling ewe-lambs (ἀμνάς). PALL.: Tell then, and before the others, what is between, and what difference one would say of the sacrifice of salvation and of the whole-burnt-offering. CYR.: Hear then. The whole-burnt-offerings of the animals, whole through wholes, were burned down (καταφλέγω) with sacred and unquenchable (ἄσβεστος) fire, nothing of the whole being taken out (ἐξαιρέω), but as it were every portion (μόριον) and limb (μέλος) going up into an odour of fragrance (ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας) to God; but the things slaughtered for the sacrifice of salvation received a partial consecration (μερικὴ καθιέρωσις), as in right shoulder (ὦμος δεξιός), head and feet, kidneys and liver, and certain others of the inward and entrails (ἐνδόσθια). It befits (πρέπει) Christ to be whole-burnt (ὁλοκαυτοῦσθαι); for He is truly wholly holy (ὅλος ἅγιος), all fragrant and sacred (ἱερός). But proper (οἰκεῖον) to us is the not-altogether holy and not-wholly sacred, in whom there is something also of defilement (μολυσμός) through the sin (ἁμαρτία) in us. 'For no one is clean from filth (ῥύπος)', and 'Transgressions (παραπτώματα) who will understand (συνίημι)?' according to what is written. Therefore the law very well ordered that the sacrifice of salvation must be consecrated not whole-burnt but rather partially. Is then, O Palladius, the account clear (σαφής) to you and sufficient (ἀποχρῶν) for easy learning (εὐμαθία)? PALL.: Very much. CYR.: Come then, let us go to that: to say something about each, I mean, of the things offered, and indeed to understand (συνίημι) the things necessary for profit (ὄνησις). PALL.: Go then. CYR.: The things from each of the tribal leaders (φύλαρχος) are one silver dish and one cup, and both full of fine flour kneaded with oil. The dish serves the edibles and is useful for eating relish (ὀψοφαγία), as the Savior Himself taught John the true (γνήσιος) disciple, who was eager to inquire (φιλοπευστέω; PG prints φιλοπνευστοῦντι), who would hand Him over (παραδίδωμι): 'The one who dipped (ἐμβάπτω) with Me the hand in the dish.' Of the cup, what would I say the use, the matter crying out (διακράζω) thus? And a sign (σημεῖον) of bread is fine flour, since bread is also from it, and bread of life (ἄρτος ζωῆς) is Christ. So as in the dish and in the cup, and as in the bread in both (for they were full of fine flour), as in food (βρῶσις) and drink (πόσις), Christ is signified (σημαίνω) as life (ζωή) and life-making (ζωοποιός). 'For amen, He says, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh (σάρξ) of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you do not have life in yourselves.' And it says the fine flour was soaked (καταδεύω) with oil, the type (τύπος) as it were singing-up (ἀναμελῳδέω) that very thing in the Psalms: 'You loved righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) and hated injustice (ἀδικία); therefore God, your God, anointed (χρίω) you with oil…' [continues in §32]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …each, one silver dish and one cup, both, it says, full of fine flour mixed with oil; one incense dish full of incense; one ram and one yearling lamb for a whole burnt offering; a male goat for sin (Numbers 7:13–16). These are the whole burnt offerings. And for a sacrifice of salvation, it says, they also brought two heifers, five rams, five he-goats and five yearling ewe lambs (Numbers 7:17).
Palladius: Explain, then, before anything else, what separates the two: what difference would one say there is between the sacrifice of salvation and the whole burnt offering?

Cyril: Listen, then. In the whole burnt offerings the animals were burned up entire by the sacred and unquenchable fire, no part at all held back; every portion and every limb rose, as it were, to God as a fragrant aroma. But the animals slaughtered for the sacrifice of salvation received a partial consecration, in the right shoulder, for example, the head and the feet, the kidneys and the liver, and certain other inner parts and entrails. It is fitting, then, that Christ should be offered as a whole burnt offering, for he is truly holy in his entirety, wholly fragrant and sacred. But to us belongs what is not altogether holy and not entirely sacred, for there is some defilement in us too, because of the sin that is in us. For ‘no one is clean from filth’ (Job 14:4), and ‘Who will understand his transgressions?’ (Psalm 19:12), as it is written. For this reason the law very rightly commanded that the sacrifice of salvation be consecrated not as a whole burnt offering, but rather in part. Is the account clear to you, then, Palladius, and enough to make it easy to grasp?
Cyril: Come, then, let us go on to the next point: to say something, I mean, about each of the things offered, and also to understand what is needed for our benefit.

Cyril: The gifts from each of the tribal leaders, then, are one silver dish and one cup, both full of fine flour mixed with oil. The dish serves for food and is useful for eating what goes with bread, as the Savior himself showed when he told John, his true disciple, who was eager to learn it, who would betray him: ‘He who dipped his hand in the dish with me,’ he says (Matthew 26:23). And why should I speak of the use of the cup, when the thing itself cries it aloud? Fine flour is a sign of bread, since bread is made from it, and the bread of life is Christ (John 6:35). So in the dish and the cup, as it were, and in the bread that was in both (for both were full of fine flour), as in food and drink, Christ is signified as life and as the giver of life. ‘For truly,’ he says, ‘I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves’ (John 6:53). And it says that the fine flour was soaked in oil, as though the type were singing out that very word in the Psalms (Psalm 45:7): ‘You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil…

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Cyril, De adoratione Book 10. Translated afresh from the PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; column may cut mid-sentence.

Section opens mid-sentence; §30 ends 'Then from' (Εἶτα παρ'), so 'each brought' supplies the verb. The quotation is from the leaders' gifts in Numbers 7 (each day's list, e.g. 7:13–17); Cyril's list here leaves out the young bull (μόσχος) of 7:15, though he treats the calf in §32. LXX Numbers 7:17 has 'two heifers' (δαμάλεις) and 'ewe lambs' (ἀμνάδας) where the Hebrew has oxen and male lambs; 'heifers' is kept because Cyril's exegesis in §§32–34 depends on the female. θυσία σωτηρίου is the LXX term for the peace offering; rendered 'sacrifice of salvation' because Cyril builds on 'salvation' (see §34). θυΐσκη (LXX; RSV 'golden dish' for incense) rendered 'incense dish'. The partial consecration list (right shoulder, head, feet, kidneys, liver, inner parts) is Cyril's own summary and does not match any single verse (compare Leviticus 3:3–4; 7:32), so no citation. 'Unquenchable fire' recalls Leviticus 6:13 but is left uncited. Job 14:4 LXX reads 'Who will be clean from filth? Not one'; Cyril paraphrases. Psalm 19:12 = LXX Psalm 18:13. The dish saying matches Matthew 26:23 word for word (compare Mark 14:20), but Cyril sets it in John's question (John 13:23–26); cited to Matthew. PG φιλοπνευστοῦντι is read as φιλοπευστοῦντι ('eager to inquire'); a doubtful reading. ὀψοφαγία ('eating relish, cooked food with bread') rendered 'eating what goes with bread'. Psalm 45:7 = LXX Psalm 44:8; the quotation runs on into §32, and the citation is placed beside 'in the Psalms' here and at the close of the quotation in §32.
